title: KPMG Opens Bengaluru Sports Tech Hub as It Eyes a $40 Billion Indian Sports Industry by 2030
excerpt: The hub, launched November 13, will build AI and data products for athlete performance, talent identification and fan engagement. KPMG values India's sports industry at about $21 billion today.
body:
• KPMG in India launched a dedicated Sports Technology Hub in Bengaluru on November 13, 2026.
  • The hub will develop AI, data analytics and digital platform products for athlete performance, talent identification, stadium management, fan engagement and large-scale sporting events.
  • KPMG estimates India's sports industry at about $21 billion today, growing at 12-14% a year, and projects it to reach $40 billion by 2030; sports technology accounts for about $1.2 billion of the current total.
  • About 250 professionals already work across KPMG's sports technology and related areas. No separate investment figure for the hub was disclosed; funding comes through existing service lines.

KPMG in India has opened a Sports Technology Hub in Bengaluru, betting that the next phase of growth in Indian sport will be bought as software: performance data, talent-scouting systems and fan platforms.

The hub, launched on November 13 by KPMG in India CEO Yezdi Nagporewalla and Indian Olympic Association President P. T. Usha, will focus on technology solutions powered by artificial intelligence, data analytics and digital platforms, according to Ascendants' report of the launch. Its work areas are athlete performance, talent identification, stadium management, fan engagement and the management of large-scale sporting events.

The $40 billion projection behind the hub

Speaking to Moneycontrol, Prasanth Shanthakumaran, Partner and Head of Sports Sector at KPMG in India, put the country's sports industry at about $21 billion today, "growing at around 12 to 14 percent" a year — almost twice the pace of overall economic growth. KPMG projects the industry to reach $40 billion by 2030.

"We are about $21 billion in the sports industry right now, growing at around 12 to 14 percent."

— Prasanth Shanthakumaran, Partner and Head of Sports Sector, KPMG in India

Within that total, KPMG estimates sports technology at approximately $1.2 billion today — the slice the Bengaluru hub is built to serve. Shanthakumaran pointed to two calendar anchors for the investment case: the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad and India's potential bid to host the 2036 Olympic Games, both of which would require the venue, data and event-management systems the hub intends to build.

Build, not buy — and no separate cheque

A major focus of the hub will be building proprietary AI capabilities rather than relying entirely on external technology providers, SightsIn Plus reported. KPMG currently has around 250 professionals working across sports technology and related areas.

The firm has not disclosed a separate investment commitment for the hub; funding will come through its existing service lines. That makes the hub a reorganisation and expansion of an existing practice, rather than a new capital project — its success will be measured in client mandates from leagues, federations and venue operators, not in a headline investment number.

What to watch

The hub's first public test is whether Indian leagues and federations buy integrated performance and fan platforms from a consultancy, rather than building in-house or buying from specialist sports-tech startups. The 2030 Commonwealth Games programme in Ahmedabad is the nearest large deadline against which that question will be answered.
